design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of proportions (R metafor; the Methods name both binomial modelling and the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation without saying which was used) of the prevalence of cannabis withdrawal syndrome (CWS) among people with regular use of cannabinoids or a cannabis use disorder (CUD). 47 articles reporting 50 cohorts and 23,518 participants (15 population-based, 28 outpatient and 7 inpatient cohorts), searched to 19 June 2019; subgroup analyses by sample source, design, timeframe, ascertainment, CUD criteria, sex and region, and 8 univariable study-level meta-regressions. Regular use was not defined by the review: each cohort's own definition was accepted.
can_establish: How often withdrawal, as each study defined it, was reported in published observational samples of people with regular use or CUD up to mid-2019, and how strongly the reported prevalence depends on where the sample came from (general population, outpatient, inpatient), on whether lifetime or past-year withdrawal was counted, and on study design.
cannot_establish: What share of people who use cannabis regularly in the general population will experience withdrawal: the headline 47% is close to the unweighted mean of the 50 cohort estimates (47.5%, editors' calculation from Table 1) and is driven by small clinical samples, while the crude proportion of all participants is 27.5% (also an editors' calculation) and population samples pool to 17%. Nor can it show which frequency, amount, potency or duration of use carries what risk (exposure was neither defined nor synthesized), how severe or long withdrawal is, whether the symptoms exceed their background rate in people who do not use cannabis (there is no comparison group), or which factors cause withdrawal (the meta-regressions are univariable and study-level).

sample.recruitment: Eight databases (MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Web of Science, AMED, CINAHL, ProQuest, Psychiatry Online) from inception to 19 June 2019, reference lists of included articles and PubMed similar-articles; English only; abstracts alone not considered (Methods, 1st paragraph). The included cohorts (Table 1) are general-population surveys (15, one of them a French national prison survey, Lukasiewicz et al. 2007), outpatient samples (28: treatment seekers, non-treatment-seeking research volunteers, detained adolescents, adolescents with conduct symptoms, adults with schizophrenia or ADHD, and people using medical cannabis for chronic pain, Perron et al. 2019) and inpatient samples (7, among them inpatient detoxification, a closed residential setting with sustained abstinence, Lee et al. 2014, and a synthetic-cannabinoid detoxification sample, Macfarlane & Christie 2015). Countries in Table 1 (editors' count): United States 37, Australia 4, Germany 3, France 2, and Brazil, Canada, the Netherlands and New Zealand 1 each.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: English-language observational studies (cohort or cross-sectional) whose primary group had regular use of cannabinoids (cannabis or synthetic cannabinoids) or CUD, and that reported the prevalence of CWS or CWS symptoms measured with a validated instrument. Excluded: case reports and series, and abstracts. Where several reports used the same sample, the most detailed was included (Methods, 2nd paragraph). The Methods say the definition of regular use varied between cohorts and is summarised in Table 1, but Table 1 has no such column.
sample.demographics: Of 23,518 participants, 16,839 (72%) were white and 14,387 men (printed as 69%; 61% by the editors' calculation). Age is printed as median (SD) 29.9 (9.0) years, which equals the unweighted mean and SD of the 48 cohort mean ages in Table 1 (editors' calculation; cohort means 15.8 to 58.5 years). 25 cohorts (50%) were treatment-seeking; cohort sizes ranged from 12 to 2,613 (Abstract › Results; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Adequacy of follow-up was reported by 7 of the 50 studies (14%) (Results, 9th paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Clinical cohorts are 35 of 50 but hold only 26% of participants (6,043 of 23,518 by Table 1, 25.7%, editors' calculation; 6,041 with the text's 357 inpatients), and with I2 at 99.2% the random-effects model weights cohorts almost equally, so small clinical samples drive the overall estimate. The inpatient group mixes treatment detoxification with a closed residential setting of sustained abstinence and prospective symptom monitoring (Lee et al. 2014; Bonnet et al. 2014; Milin et al. 2008, by their titles), and includes a synthetic-cannabinoid withdrawal sample; the population group includes a prison survey. By their titles, two population cohorts analysed the same national survey (Agrawal et al. 2008 and Hasin et al. 2008, both NESARC), although the review states that one report per sample was kept. English-only search, no grey literature.

exposure.measurement: Each cohort's own definition of regular use or CUD. CUD by DSM-III-R (8 cohorts), DSM-IV (37) or DSM-5 (5) according to Table 2; Table 1 lists 38 DSM-IV and 4 DSM-5 cohorts (editors' count). The proportion of each cohort with CUD ranged from 1.8% to 100% (Table 1). No common definition of regular use is given, and fewer than half of the cohorts reported baseline cannabis intake (Results, 1st paragraph), yet the proportion using daily enters a meta-regression with 48 studies (Table 3); the source of those percentages is not explained.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized: no amounts, frequency categories, duration, potency, product or route. The authors note that changing products, which may affect tolerance, dependence and withdrawal, could not be addressed, and that few studies measured cannabinoids in urine or blood (Strengths and Limitations).
exposure.polysubstance: Handled only as study-level covariates in univariable meta-regressions: the proportion with tobacco use (26 studies; β 0.002, P = .02), other drug use (11 studies; β 0.003, P = .05), alcohol use (17; P = .97) and psychiatric disorder (16; P = .93) (Table 3; Table 3 heads these as the percentage with a disorder, the Results text as comorbid use). Tobacco withdrawal shares several symptoms with CWS (irritability, anxiety, sleep and appetite change), and the review cannot separate them because it has no individual-level data.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Varies by design and is not synthesized: recall of lifetime withdrawal in surveys (18 cohorts), past-year withdrawal (32), and prospective symptom ratings during enforced abstinence in some residential and inpatient studies. Where a study offered several cut points, the review took the lowest threshold for CWS (Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph), which pushes prevalence up.

comparison.controls: None. Prevalence is reported without any group of people who do not use cannabis or who did not cut down, so the background frequency of irritability, anxiety, sleep and appetite problems is not subtracted. The introduction names the comparison with the general population as an open question (Introduction, 3rd paragraph); the review does not address it.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Pre-existing anxiety, mood and sleep problems, tobacco dependence and other drug use at the individual level; study-level meta-regressions cannot separate these from withdrawal.

outcomes.instruments: Clinician-administered scales (for example the Cannabis Withdrawal Scale), self-report checklists (Marijuana Withdrawal Checklist, Marijuana Quit Questionnaire) and diagnostic interviews (SCID, SSAGA, CIDI-SAM, AUDADIS, DIGS, Customary Drinking and Drug Use Record), and timeline follow-back (Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1). Table 1 lists operationalized criteria for 5 cohorts and a self-reported diary for 1.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors note generally poor correlation between rating scales and no consensus on the best tool (Discussion, 7th paragraph). Study quality by the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (scored out of 8): 36 studies (72%) fair, 2 (4%) good, 12 (24%) poor; the per-study ratings are in the supplement (not read).
outcomes.operationalization: CWS as each study defined it. DSM-5, as summarised in the introduction, requires at least 3 of 7 symptoms within 7 days of reduced use; most cohorts predate DSM-5 and used research definitions. Lifetime and past-year prevalence were pooled together in the overall estimate, and the lowest available threshold was used.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 28 = 1 overall pooled estimate, 19 subgroup estimates in Table 2 (7 subgroup factors) and 8 univariable meta-regressions in Table 3; a treatment-seeking comparison is reported only as a test statistic, and leave-one-out and publication-bias analyses are in the supplement.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles and abstracts were screened by one reviewer, with a second checking everything marked as excluded; full texts by two independent reviewers, with a third for unresolved disagreements; extraction by one reviewer, checked by a second; quality rating by one, double-checked by a second (Methods, 2nd, 3rd and 6th paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled prevalence (random effects): overall 47% (Abstract: 95% CI 41% to 52%; Results text: 27% to 37%), 50 cohorts, I2 99.2%, cohort range 8% to 100%. By sample source: population-based 17% (13% to 21%; Table 2: 13 to 22), 15 cohorts, 17,475 participants, I2 98%; outpatient 54% (48% to 59%), 28 cohorts, 5,684 participants, I2 92% in the text and 94% in Table 2; inpatient 87% (79% to 94%), 7 cohorts, 357 participants, I2 74% in the text and 94% in Table 2. Design: cross-sectional 19% (15% to 24%), 17 cohorts; cohort 62% (56% to 68%), 33. Timeframe: past year 31% (27% to 36%), 32 cohorts; lifetime 76% (70% to 82%), 18. Ascertainment: clinician-rated 52% (41% to 62%), 20; self-reported 45% (37% to 53%), 23; informant-rated 40% (21% to 59%), 7 (P = .49). CUD criteria: DSM-IV 49% (43% to 56%), 37; DSM-III-R 45% (31% to 58%), 8; DSM-5 34% (15% to 54%), 5 (P = .44). Sex: men 27% (21% to 34%), women 26% (19% to 33%), 15 studies each (P = .99). Region: North America 48% (42% to 55%), 38; Europe 47% (25% to 70%), 6; South America 51% (44% to 59%), 1; Australasia 36% (20% to 52%), 5 (P = .77). Univariable meta-regressions (slope per percentage point of the covariate; scale not stated): % with CUD β 0.005 (48 studies, P < .001; intercept 0.128); % using daily β 0.004 (48, P < .001; intercept 0.151); % tobacco β 0.002 (26, P = .02); % other drugs β 0.003 (11, P = .05); alcohol, psychiatric disorder, mean age (β −0.007, P = .10) and % white not associated. Editors' calculation from Table 1: crude proportion of participants with withdrawal 27.5% (6,470 of 23,518; the abstract's count is 6,469); unweighted mean of the 50 cohort prevalences 47.5%; crude proportion in population-based cohorts 18.6%. No prediction intervals or tau2 are reported.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Each meta-regression has a single covariate; there is no multivariable model, so setting, the share with CUD, daily use and tobacco use, which travel together across cohorts, cannot be separated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The Methods state that an a priori protocol was used, citing reference 13, which is the PROSPERO home page (accessed 24 November 2019, after the June 2019 search) with no registration number; the protocol cannot be checked. PRISMA reporting is stated.
analysis.selective_reporting: Subgroups planned for intensity of use, psychiatric comorbidity and age were run as meta-regressions where subgroup estimates were not available, and the age- and sex-specific prevalence estimates named as an aim in the introduction are reported only as the 15-study sex comparison. The treatment-seeking comparison is given only as a test statistic (χ2 = 446.32, P < .001), without the two prevalences. Leave-one-out and publication-bias results are summarised in one sentence each, with the details in the supplement (not read).
analysis.power: Not addressed. The inpatient estimate rests on 7 cohorts with 357 participants, the DSM-5 estimate on 5 cohorts, the other-drug meta-regression on 11 studies and the South American estimate on 1 study.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Reported withdrawal prevalence varies enormously with the sample: about 17% in general-population samples of people with regular use (15 cohorts holding three-quarters of all participants), about 54% in outpatient samples and 87% in 7 small inpatient or residential samples; past-year prevalence (31%) is far below lifetime prevalence (76%). Heterogeneity is extreme (I2 99.2% overall, 74% to 98% within settings). Across all 23,518 participants, 27.5% had withdrawal by their study's definition (editors' calculation); the pooled 47% is essentially the average of the cohort estimates. Prevalence did not differ between men and women (27% and 26%). At study level, cohorts with more CUD, more daily use or more tobacco use reported more withdrawal.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points and abstract present 47% as the prevalence of CWS among people with regular or dependent use, and the Discussion (1st paragraph) says withdrawal will be experienced by "nearly half (47%) of all people with regular or dependent cannabinoid use". Gaps: (1) 47% is not a population prevalence but the near-unweighted mean of mostly clinical cohorts; the participant-level proportion is 27.5% (editors' calculation) and the general-population estimate 17%, and the abstract itself pairs 47% with a count (6,469 of 23,518) that equals 27.5%; (2) lifetime and past-year prevalence, and research definitions of withdrawal from before DSM-5, are pooled into one number; (3) the Conclusions state that withdrawal was more common in men, contradicting the review's own result (27% against 26%, P = .99); (4) study-level univariable meta-regressions are reported as factors associated with withdrawal in people, and the association with CUD is partly definitional, since the abstract itself calls withdrawal a diagnostic indicator of CUD; (5) the Discussion (2nd paragraph) suggests that withdrawal symptoms may be mistaken for anxiety or depression that people treat with cannabis, which the review did not study. On the other side, the Results and Discussion do report the setting-specific estimates, and the Strengths and Limitations section names the heterogeneity of instruments as the main limitation.

timeline.event: Budney, Novy & Hughes: withdrawal among adults seeking treatment for marijuana dependence; one of the studies by Budney and colleagues that, in the review's account, first proposed the syndrome (included cohort, 57.4%).
Budney et al.: time course and significance of cannabis withdrawal (included cohort, 77.8%).
Budney et al. (Am J Psychiatry): review of the validity and significance of cannabis withdrawal syndrome, among the sources cited for earlier estimates of 11.1% to 94.2%.
Hasin et al. (34.4%) and Agrawal et al. (8.0%): two general-population analyses of the US NESARC survey, both included as separate cohorts.
Allsop et al.: development of the Cannabis Withdrawal Scale, cited as a clinician-administered instrument.
DSM-5 recognises cannabis withdrawal (at least 3 of 7 symptoms within 7 days of reduced use), as described in the review's introduction.
Livne et al.: DSM-5 cannabis withdrawal syndrome in US adults, the only DSM-5 general-population cohort in the review (12.1%).
This review: by its authors' account the largest systematic review and the first meta-analysis of cannabis withdrawal prevalence.

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of cannabis withdrawal prevalence that this review knows of. Its usable product is the setting-specific estimates, above all about one in six people with regular use in general-population samples (17%, from 15 cohorts with different definitions of regular use and of withdrawal, I2 98%), not the 47% headline. No later synthesis was read for this card. For the related question of how many people who use cannabis develop a use disorder, see the project's card for Leung et al. (2020) (sc_leung_2020). Primary cohorts inside the pools (for example Hasin et al. 2008, Agrawal et al. 2008 and Livne et al. 2019) must not be cited as independent support alongside this review.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement, although the author contributions list Seitz as having obtained funding.
funding.declared_conflicts: Bahji: a Canadian Institutes of Health Research Master's Student scholarship while the manuscript was drafted. Seitz: site investigator for a clinical trial sponsored by Hoffmann La Roche. No other disclosures were reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Queen's University (Kingston, Ontario) and the University of Calgary. No author of the review wrote an included primary study; the first author's earlier reviews were the models for the extraction form (references 12, 61 and 62). A librarian helped develop the search (Additional Contributions).

what_would_settle_it: Prospective general-population cohorts of people who use cannabis, with frequency, amount, product and potency measured, in which DSM-5 withdrawal is assessed with one validated instrument during actual reductions or quit attempts, compared with people who keep using unchanged and with people who do not use (to subtract background symptoms and tobacco withdrawal), reporting prevalence by pattern of use; in the meantime, an individual-participant meta-analysis of the existing DSM-5 surveys with common definitions.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with regular or dependent use of cannabinoids), outcome (CWS prevalence measured with a validated instrument) and designs (observational) are stated; a prevalence question needs no comparator. Regular use is not defined.

The Methods say an a priori protocol was used, but the citation is the PROSPERO home page, accessed after the search, with no registration number; the protocol's content and timing cannot be verified and deviations are not discussed. A close call against partial yes.
Observational designs suit a prevalence question, but the choice, and the exclusion of case reports and series, is not explained.

Eight databases, reference lists and PubMed similar-articles, with librarian input and the strategy in eTable 1 (not read); but English only and abstracts excluded, with no grey literature, and neither limit is justified, which is no under decision p-amstar2-item4.

Titles and abstracts were screened by one reviewer, with every excluded record checked by a second; full texts were screened independently by two, with a third for disagreements (Methods, 2nd paragraph). A close call, judged met because every exclusion was seen by two people.
Extraction by one reviewer, checked by a second (the abstract says in duplicate) (Methods, 3rd paragraph); two reviewers' consensus meets the item's first criterion, as in sc_mcketin_2019.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The 39 full-text exclusions (86 read, 47 included) appear only in the PRISMA flowchart, an image that was not read; the supplement's listed contents include no list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives setting, CUD and CWS criteria, size, % with CUD, % men, age and prevalence for each cohort; the definition of regular use, frequency of use, timeframe (lifetime or past-year) and design of each cohort are not given in the article (study characteristics are in eTable 2, not read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, summed to a score and grouped good, fair or poor, checked by a second reviewer; it covers representativeness and ascertainment, but most of its items (non-exposed cohort, comparability, follow-up) do not fit prevalence studies, and response rates and the validity of the withdrawal measure are not assessed. Per-study ratings are in the supplement.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling of proportions, but general-population, outpatient and inpatient cohorts and lifetime and past-year prevalence are combined into one headline estimate at I2 99.2% without a stated reason and without a prediction interval; the transformation used is not stated; the interval of the overall estimate differs between abstract and text, and the between-group test statistics cannot correspond to their P values. Consistent with SENIOR-DECISIONS item 25 (Murrie et al. 2020: proportions pooled at I2 near 99% without a stated reason).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis by quality rating; the leave-one-out analysis (supplement) concerns single studies, not risk of bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Strengths and Limitations section counts the mostly fair quality as a strength, and the Discussion does not consider how sample selection, recall of lifetime withdrawal or the lowest-threshold rule could bias the estimates.

Subgroups (sample source, design, timeframe, ascertainment, criteria, sex, region) and meta-regressions investigated heterogeneity, and the limitations name the range of instruments as its main source; heterogeneity within subgroups nevertheless remained between 74% and 99%.

Funnel plots, rank-correlation and Egger tests and trim-and-fill (eFigure 2, not read), reported as showing no evidence of bias. Such tests have limited meaning for prevalence estimates, which carry no direction that favours publication.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors' conflicts are declared, but no funding statement names the source of the funding that the contributions say Seitz obtained.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence when more than one critical item is not met: items 2 (protocol not verifiable), 4 (unjustified English-only search without grey literature), 7 (no list of excluded studies), 11 (one headline estimate pooled across incompatible samples and timeframes at I2 99.2%) and 13 (study quality not considered in the interpretation) are not met, item 9 is partly met and only item 15 is met. In practice, the setting-specific estimates, and above all the general-population estimate of 17%, are the usable results, with the caveat that definitions differ between cohorts; the overall 47% must not be cited as the share of people with regular use who experience withdrawal. The review may be cited for the range of reported prevalence by setting and timeframe and as a pointer to primary cohorts.

key_findings.finding: The search to 19 June 2019 found 3,848 unique records; 86 full texts were read and 47 articles included, reporting 50 cohorts with 23,518 participants: 15 population-based (30%), 28 outpatient (56%) and 7 inpatient (14%) cohorts; 25 cohorts (50%) were treatment-seeking and 38 came from North America; cohort sizes ranged from 12 to 2,613. 18 cohorts reported lifetime and 32 past-year withdrawal.

Overall pooled prevalence of cannabis withdrawal syndrome (random effects): 47%, I2 99.2%, 50 cohorts, 23,518 participants; the cohort estimates ranged from 8% to 100%. The abstract gives the 95% CI as 41% to 52% and the count as 6,469 of 23,518.
key_findings.note: The Results text gives the interval as 27% to 37%, which does not contain 47%. The count of 6,469 of 23,518 is 27.5% (editors' calculation), the participant-level proportion; 47% is the random-effects mean across cohorts. Do not describe 47% as the share of participants or of people with regular use. Figure 2 (forest plot, read as an image) prints a third version of the overall estimate, random effects 0.46 (0.37 to 0.55), and a fixed-effect total of 0.28 (0.27 to 0.28), which gives larger cohorts more weight; its event column sums to the abstract's 6,469 (second reader's count), so the review itself prints a participant-level figure of about 28%.

key_findings.finding: By sample source: population-based samples 17% (95% CI 13% to 21%), 15 cohorts, 17,475 participants, I2 98%; outpatient samples 54% (48% to 59%), 28 cohorts, 5,684 participants; inpatient samples 87% (79% to 94%), 7 cohorts, 357 participants; the difference between settings is reported as P < .001.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results, 5th paragraph; Table 2 (Sample source)
key_findings.note: Table 2 prints the population interval as 13 to 22, and the 4th paragraph of the Results gives 0.16 (0.13 to 0.20); within-setting I2 is 92% (outpatient) and 74% (inpatient) in the text but 94% for both in Table 2; Figure 2 agrees with the text (98%, 92%, 74%) and gives the inpatient total as 359. The population-based cohorts hold 74% of all participants (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Past-year withdrawal 31% (27% to 36%; 32 cohorts) against lifetime withdrawal 76% (70% to 82%; 18 cohorts); cross-sectional studies 19% (15% to 24%; 17 cohorts) against cohort studies 62% (56% to 68%; 33); treatment-seeking samples higher than others (χ2 = 446.32, P < .001; the two prevalences are not given).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 2 (Study design; Timeline of CWS)

key_findings.finding: No detectable differences by method of ascertainment (clinician-rated 52%, 41% to 62%, 20 cohorts; self-reported 45%, 37% to 53%, 23; informant-rated 40%, 21% to 59%, 7; P = .49), by CUD criteria (DSM-IV 49%, 43% to 56%, 37; DSM-III-R 45%, 31% to 58%, 8; DSM-5 34%, 15% to 54%, 5; P = .44) or by region (North America 48%, 42% to 55%, 38; Europe 47%, 25% to 70%, 6; South America 51%, 44% to 59%, 1 study; Australasia 36%, 20% to 52%, 5; P = .77).
key_findings.note: Each comparison is between groups of studies, not people, and is confounded by sample source and timeframe.

key_findings.finding: In the 15 studies reporting estimates by sex, withdrawal prevalence was 27% (21% to 34%) in men and 26% (19% to 33%) in women (P = .99); no association was found with age, race or ethnicity, method of ascertainment, CUD criteria, alcohol use, psychiatric comorbidity or region.
key_findings.note: The Conclusions nevertheless say withdrawal was more common in men (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Univariable study-level meta-regressions: higher withdrawal prevalence in cohorts with a larger share of participants with CUD (β 0.005, 48 studies, P < .001), using cannabis daily (β 0.004, 48, P < .001), using tobacco (β 0.002, 26, P = .02) or using other drugs (β 0.003, 11, P = .05); no association with the share with alcohol use (17 studies, P = .97) or psychiatric disorder (16, P = .93), mean age (β −0.007, 48, P = .10) or the share of white participants (42, P = .46).
key_findings.note: Slopes are per percentage point and the scale is not stated (the intercepts, 0.128 for CUD and 0.151 for daily use, suggest the proportion scale). Table 3 heads these covariates as the percentage with a disorder, the text as comorbid use. These are ecological associations between study characteristics; the CUD association is partly definitional, since withdrawal counts towards a DSM-5 CUD diagnosis. P = .05 is not below the paper's stated significance threshold of .05.

key_findings.finding: Study quality (Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, maximum 8 points): 36 of 50 studies (72%) fair, 2 (4%) good and 12 (24%) poor; ascertainment of exposure was met by 36 studies (72%) and comparability by 26 (52%), while absence of the outcome at the start was shown by 3 (6%) and adequate follow-up by 7 (14%).

Leave-one-out analyses did not change the pooled prevalence substantially, and funnel plots, rank-correlation and Egger tests and trim-and-fill showed no evidence of publication bias (figures in eFigure 2 of the supplement, not read).

34.7% of participants (n = 8,275) had CUD by each study's criteria; the Results give ranges for this proportion of 8% to 34% (population), 30% to 74% (outpatient) and 72% to 98% (inpatient); fewer than half of the cohorts reported baseline cannabis intake.
key_findings.note: 8,275 of 23,518 is 35.2% (editors' calculation), and the ranges do not match the CUD column of Table 1 (see reporting issues); take cohort values from Table 1.

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from Table 1 (cohort size multiplied by prevalence, summed over the 50 rows): 6,470 of 23,518 participants (27.5%) had withdrawal, matching the abstract's 6,469; the unweighted mean of the 50 cohort prevalences is 47.5% (median 49.1%), which the pooled 47% approximates; crude proportions are 18.6% in population-based, 51.5% in outpatient and 82.2% in inpatient cohorts. Clinical cohorts are 35 of 50 but hold 26% of participants.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation. With I2 at 99.2% the random-effects weights are nearly equal, so the pooled estimate tracks the average cohort rather than the average participant. The review's own Figure 2 prints a fixed-effect total of 0.28 (0.27 to 0.28), close to this participant-level proportion.

key_findings.finding: General-population cohorts in Table 1 (size; prevalence): Cottler et al. 1995 (102; 15.7%), Wiesbeck et al. 1996 (1,735; 15.6%), Swift et al. 1998 (243; 20.2%), Swift et al. 2001 (722; 29.5%), Nocon et al. 2006 (732; 16.1%), Lukasiewicz et al. 2007, a French prison survey (278; 7.6%), Agrawal et al. 2008 (1,603; 8.0%), Hasin et al. 2008 (2,613; 34.4%), Ehlers et al. 2010 (818; 16.5%), Smith et al. 2013 (1,712 and 1,187; 18.8% and 9.8%), Verweij et al. 2013 (2,276; 11.9%), Delforterie et al. 2015 (United States 1,568, 29.2%; the Netherlands 359, 12.5%) and Livne et al. 2019, the only DSM-5 population cohort (1,527; 12.1%).

Inpatient cohorts in Table 1 (size; prevalence): Milin et al. 2008 (21 adolescents; 100%), Vandrey et al. 2008 (12; 100%), Preuss et al. 2010 (118; 72.0%), Dervaux et al. 2011 (92; 84.8%), Bonnet et al. 2014 (39; 92.3%), Lee et al. 2014 (30; 73.3%) and Macfarlane & Christie 2015 (47; 87.2%). By their titles, Lee et al. studied people who smoked cannabis chronically and frequently during sustained abstinence within a closed residential environment, Vandrey et al. was a within-person comparison of abstinence from cannabis and tobacco, and Macfarlane & Christie concerns synthetic-cannabinoid withdrawal in a detoxification service.

As summarised in the introduction, DSM-5 cannabis withdrawal requires at least 3 of 7 symptoms developing within 7 days of reduced use: irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep disturbance; appetite or weight disturbance; restlessness; depressed mood; and somatic symptoms such as headache, sweating, nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain. Where a study used several cut points, the review took the lowest threshold.

Second-hand figures: earlier estimates of withdrawal prevalence ranged from 11.1% to 94.2% (citing Budney et al. 2004; Hasin 2018; Anthony et al. 2017; Bahji & Mazhar 2016, the first author's review); previous reviews are said to report withdrawal symptoms in about one-third of people with regular use in the general population (citing Budney & Hughes 2006; Agrawal et al. 2008; Hasin et al. 2008) and in 50% to 95% of people with heavy use in treatment or research studies (citing Copersino et al. 2006; Chung et al. 2008; Cornelius et al. 2008; Levin et al. 2010).
key_findings.note: Second-hand; several of the cited primary studies are also inside the review's pools, and the 11.1% to 94.2% range is not attributed to particular studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The overall pooled prevalence of 47% is given with a 95% CI of 41% to 52% in the abstract but 27% to 37% in the Results text; the second interval does not contain the point estimate. Figure 2 prints a third version, random effects 0.46 (0.37 to 0.55).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the abstract interval for the random-effects estimate; the 27% to 37% interval may belong to another quantity (the crude participant-level proportion is 27.5%).

reporting_issues.issue: The setting estimates appear in three versions: 17% (13% to 21%) in the abstract and Results 5th paragraph, 17 (13 to 22) in Table 2, and 0.16 (0.13 to 0.20) in the Results 4th paragraph, which also gives 0.87 (0.77 to 0.93) instead of 87 (79 to 94) for inpatients and labels both the 0.54 and the 0.87 estimates as inpatient.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Small differences, but a claim should quote one version (Table 2) and the outpatient figure is 0.54, not inpatient.

reporting_issues.issue: Within-setting heterogeneity is given as I2 92% (outpatient) and 74% (inpatient) in the Results text but 94% for both in Table 2. Figure 2 prints the inpatient heterogeneity as chi-square 11.41 on 6 degrees of freedom (P < .08) with I2 74%; that chi-square corresponds to I2 of about 47% and P = .077 (editors' calculation), so heterogeneity among the 7 inpatient cohorts was not significant, although the text calls it significant.
reporting_issues.consequence: The inpatient heterogeneity is reported three ways (74%, 94%, and about 47% implied by the figure's own chi-square); none can be relied on, and the inpatient interval should be read as uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The between-group test statistics cannot correspond to their P values: χ2 = 0.172 is printed with P < .001 for sample source and the identical 0.172 with P = .99 for sex; 0.194 (design) and 0.314 (timeframe) are printed with P < .001. A χ2 of 0.172 corresponds to P of about 0.68 with 1 degree of freedom or 0.92 with 2 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results, 5th paragraph; Table 2 (between-group comparison columns)
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup significance tests cannot be checked; the differences between settings and between lifetime and past-year estimates are large enough to rely on the non-overlapping intervals instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions say withdrawal was more common in men, but the review's own subgroup analysis found 27% in men and 26% in women (P = .99), and the Discussion (1st paragraph) also says withdrawal was not associated with sex, so the Conclusions contradict both.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Conclusions; Results, 5th paragraph; Table 2 (Sex)
reporting_issues.consequence: No claim of a sex difference can rest on this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results give 14,387 men as 69% of 23,518 participants; 14,387 of 23,518 is 61.2%, and the percentages in Table 1 give about 61% (13,426 of 22,064 with sex reported) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: About 61% of participants were men, not 69%.

reporting_issues.issue: Age is printed as median (SD) 29.9 (9.0) years; these values equal the unweighted mean and SD of the 48 cohort mean ages in Table 1 (editors' calculation), not a participant median.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Describe the participants as having a mean cohort age of about 30 years (cohort means 15.8 to 58.5).

reporting_issues.issue: The ranges given for the proportion with CUD (population 8% to 34%, outpatient 30% to 74%, inpatient 72% to 98%) do not match the CUD column of Table 1 (population 3.5% to 57.2%, outpatient 1.8% to 100%, inpatient 79.3% to 100%); the population range matches the withdrawal column of Table 1 (7.6% to 34.4%) instead (editors' reading of Table 1). The overall 34.7% (n = 8,275) is 35.2% of 23,518, or 40.1% of the 20,619 participants in cohorts reporting CUD (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The CUD figures in the text cannot be used; take cohort values from Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Regions are given as North America 38 (76%), Australia 7 (14%) and Europe 6 (12%), which sums to 51 cohorts and 102% and omits the Brazilian cohort; Table 1 has 4 Australian and 1 New Zealand cohort, matching the counts of 5 for Australasia and 1 for South America in Table 2. Table 2 also counts 37 DSM-IV and 5 DSM-5 cohorts where Table 1 lists 38 and 4 (editors' count).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use the subgroup counts of Table 2, which sum to 50.

reporting_issues.issue: The inpatient subgroup is given 357 participants in the text, while the inpatient rows of Table 1 sum to 359; the three settings in the text sum to 23,516, not 23,518 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible for the estimates; quote 357 as printed with the setting estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: Inclusion required a validated instrument, yet Table 1 lists the withdrawal criteria of 5 cohorts as operationalized (Budney et al. 1998; Swift et al. 1998; Schuckit et al. 1999; Swift et al. 2000; Lukasiewicz et al. 2007) and of 1 as a self-reported diary (Kouri & Pope 2000); the Results (2nd paragraph) nevertheless list references 19, 21, 22, 23, 24 and 31 among the cohorts assessed with the SCID.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Study Selection; Methods, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Measurement of withdrawal is less standardised than the inclusion criterion implies.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say each cohort's definition of regular use is summarised in Table 1, but Table 1 has no such column; and the share using daily enters a meta-regression with 48 studies although fewer than half of the cohorts reported baseline cannabis intake.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 2nd paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure behind every estimate is undocumented in the article, and the daily-use meta-regression cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The association with other drug use (β 0.003, P = .05) is reported in the abstract and Results as an association, although the Methods set significance at P < .05.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Other drug use should not be listed among the factors associated with withdrawal on this evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: By their titles, two included population cohorts analysed the same US survey, NESARC (Agrawal et al. 2008, 1,603 participants, 8.0%; Hasin et al. 2008, 2,613, 34.4%), although the Methods say that only the most detailed report of a sample was included; whether they are distinct subsamples is not explained.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; References 32 and 35
reporting_issues.consequence: Possible double counting of one survey in the population estimate; the fourfold difference between two analyses of the same survey also shows how much the definition matters.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives a mean age of 58.5 years for Hasin et al. (2008), a general-population sample of people who use cannabis; this is ten years older than any other cohort mean (the next is 48.4) and may be an entry error. It enters the age meta-regression.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 (Hasin et al. 2008 row)
reporting_issues.consequence: Unverified against the primary study; the null age association should not be leaned on.

reporting_issues.issue: The a priori protocol is cited to reference 13, the PROSPERO home page accessed on 24 November 2019, five months after the search date of 19 June 2019, with no registration number.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether and when a protocol was registered cannot be established from the article (AMSTAR 2 item 2).
